o: A pair (a, b) is perfect iff min(|a-b|, |a+b|) <= min(|a|,|b|) and max(|a-b|, |a+b|) >= max(|a|,|b|). Working out the algebra: assuming |a| <= |b|, the binding condition simplifies to |b| <= 2|a| regardless of signs (one of |a+-b| is the sum, the other the difference of absolute values; the sum always dominates and the difference condition is exactly |b|-|a| <= |a|). Zeros behave correctly: (0,0) qualifies, (0, x>0) does not. So after sorting absolute values we count pairs with larger <= 2 * smaller via two pointers.
k: The two inequalities collapse to: with |a| <= |b|, perfect iff |b| <= 2*|a|.
Signs are irrelevant; only absolute values matter.
Sort absolute values and use a monotone two-pointer window to count pairs in O(n log n).

a.i: Sort |nums|. For each i, all j > i with a[j] <= 2*a[i] form perfect pairs with i; since 2*a[i] grows with i the right boundary only moves forward, giving an amortized linear sweep after sorting.
s: Replace nums with their absolute values and sort.
Maintain pointer j starting ahead of i; extend while a[j] <= 2*a[i].
Add (j - i - 1) to the answer for each i.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the two-pointer sweep is O(n).

w: Deriving the |b| <= 2|a| characterization on paper first is the whole problem; verify against all three examples including zeros and mixed signs. Watch overflow of 2*a[i] for 1e9 inputs in 32-bit languages. Follow-up: count pairs with ratio in [1/r, r] generally — same two-pointer skeleton.
